# Concepts

Rimsky is a reactive node-graph orchestration platform. This document defines the 75 nouns rimsky's own surfaces use — its error messages, its event feed, its template schema, its API — and names, for each noun, where you meet it.

Read the definition first, then the **Where you meet it** line. That line names the classes of public surface the concept is expressed through, and gives the element names you will type or read.

## The classes of public surface

Rimsky's public surface splits into these classes. Every concept below points into one or more of them.

| Class | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| CLI verbs, CLI flags | What `rimsky` accepts. |
| HTTP routes | The control API's REST skin, under `/v1`. |
| MCP tools, MCP resources, MCP methods | The control API's daemon-facing skin, on the same port. |
| Permission actions | The strings a key's grant is written in. |
| Template keys | The YAML a template author writes. |
| Config keys | `rimsky.yml`, the supervisor's own file, and the CLI's `~/.rimsky/config.yml`. |
| Environment variables | `RIMSKY_*`, read by the binaries and the bundled service images. |
| Event kinds | The `kind` values on rows in the event feed. |
| Error classes | The class strings executors and producers emit, and templates route on. |
| gRPC RPCs, proto files | The wire contract a service implements. |
| Compose manifest keys | The keys `rimsky compose` reads. |
| Publisher kinds, publisher config keys | What a template's `publishers:` block declares. |
| Service config keys, executor attribute keys | What each bundled service image reads. |
| Binaries, images, image commands, image paths, ports | What ships and how it runs. |
| Bundled roles | The role names the CLI expands into grants. |
| Published packages | The Go modules, the npm package, and the release archives. |

Two general notes about reading the surface:

- **The CLI is not a complete cover of the API.** It is a thin client, but 32 of the control API's routes are reached by no CLI verb — the debugger, pause and resume, the diagnostics reads, and the audit feed among them. Where a concept lives only behind HTTP or MCP, the entry says so.
- **Names repeat across classes.** A template key, a config key, and an environment variable that share a word are not the same knob. Each entry names the class it means.

---

## Authoring: templates and graphs

**template** (alias: canonical-spec) — The static artifact you register: node definitions, attribute schemas, claim and lock declarations, subscription declarations, message-type schemas, publisher declarations, a params schema, late-bind service names, and sub-graph declarations. Rimsky identifies a template by a content hash over its canonicalized bytes, so two specs that differ only in key order or whitespace are the same template. Registering the same spec twice returns the existing template rather than a conflict. A template moves through register, deploy, undeploy, and deregister.

*Where you meet it:* CLI verbs `rimsky template register|lint|list|get|deploy|undeploy|rm`, and the shorthands `rimsky register|deploy|undeploy|ls templates`. HTTP routes `POST /v1/templates`, `POST /v1/templates/validate`, `GET /v1/templates`, `GET /v1/templates/{id}`, `POST /v1/templates/{id}/deploy`, `POST /v1/templates/{id}/undeploy`, `DELETE /v1/templates/{id}`. MCP tools `template_register`, `template_validate`, `template_list`, `template_get`, `template_deploy`, `template_undeploy`, `template_deregister`. Permission actions `template:read|validate|register|deploy|undeploy|deregister`. Event kinds `template_validation_failed`, `template_resolution_failed`. Template keys `name`, `version`, `description`, `params_schema`, `params_redact`, `late_bind_services`, `message_queue_mode`.

`rimsky template lint` reports the same findings registration does, and it needs no running deployment. Two template keys are worth knowing before you write one: `params_redact` suppresses a named param in `GET /v1/instances/{id}` only — the value still appears in full in `GET /v1/events`, `GET /v1/audit`, and the observability reads. And `POST /v1/tags` is not idempotent the way template and instance creation are: re-creating an existing tag answers 409.

**tag** (alias: template-tag) — A movable string alias pointing at a template hash. Operators move a tag to say "this is the current shape of this template." Moving a tag does not migrate running instances; only later instance creates pick up the new target. Unrelated to a terminal tag, which shares only the word.

*Where you meet it:* CLI verbs `rimsky tag create|list|get|mv|rm`, `rimsky ls tags`. CLI flags `--tag`, `--tag-prefix`. HTTP routes `POST /v1/tags`, `GET /v1/tags`, `PUT /v1/tags/{tag}`, `DELETE /v1/tags/{tag}`. MCP tools `tag_create`, `tag_list`, `tag_set`, `tag_delete`. Permission actions `tag:read|create|set|delete`. Compose manifest key `templates[].tag`.

**graph** — Rimsky's unit of node connectivity. A template declares graphs explicitly under `graphs:`, or implicitly by listing nodes at the top level; either form is the reserved top-level graph, named `main`. Every instance's root execution context binds to that top-level graph. Any other graph is a sub-graph.

*Where you meet it:* Template keys `graphs[].name`, `graphs[].nodes`, `nodes[]`.

**sub-graph** — A graph that declares an entry node and an exit node, invocable from another node. The calling node absorbs the entry: it dispatches with the entry's executor, and the entry never gets a run of its own. The exit stays a separate node, and its writeback flows back to the caller.

*Where you meet it:* Template keys `graphs[].entry`, `graphs[].exit`, `nodes[].delegate`. Two further template keys, `nodes[].is_subgraph_entry_absorbed` and `nodes[].is_subgraph_exit`, are set by canonicalization; declaring either in your own file is a registration error naming the key.

**node** (alias: graph-node) — One declarative unit of work in a graph. A node has a name, a type (the dispatch routing key), subscription entries, required claims and locks, co-held upstream claims, an attributes schema, operator-facing tags, per-error-class policy, and a target executor. The node row carries no runtime state — all execution state lives on node-runs. Operator surfaces summarize a node's runs into four counts: `active`, `pending`, `fresh`, `failed`.

*Where you meet it:* CLI verb `rimsky node get`. HTTP routes `GET /v1/nodes/{id}`, `POST /v1/nodes/{id}/reset`, `GET /v1/instances/{idOrKey}/nodes`. MCP tools `node_get`, `node_list`, `node_reset`. Permission actions `node:read`, `node:reset`. Template keys `nodes[].type`, `nodes[].kind`, `nodes[].description`, `nodes[].executor`, `nodes[].tags`, `nodes[].max_retries`, `nodes[].retry_backoff.*`, `nodes[].sync_rpc_deadline`, `nodes[].max_quiet_period`, `nodes[].max_runtime`.

`nodes[].tags` are real selectors, but only over HTTP: `GET /v1/instances/{id}/nodes?tag=<tag>` filters by them. The `--tag` and `--tag-prefix` CLI flags do not — they are undefined on every verb that lists nodes. And `POST /v1/nodes/{id}/reset` is narrow: it answers 409 unless the node has a failed terminal run in some scope.

**attribute** — The typed inputs, outputs, and configuration of a node, declared by a JSON Schema in `nodes[].attributes.schema`. A property is source-bound (a substitution directive resolved when the run's bag is built), static-default (resolved at registration), or executor-written (populated at commit). The substitution grammar has six source kinds: `{{claim.<alias>.address|claim_scope|payload}}`, `{{params.<key>}}`, `{{nodes.<node>.attribute...}}`, `{{messages.<type>...}}`, `{{child.partition_key}}`, and `{{env.<VAR>}}`. Rimsky validates the bag twice — after substitution at dispatch, and after writeback at commit. An executor returns an attributes delta on its settling verdict, and may also post incremental writebacks mid-dispatch.

*Where you meet it:* Template keys `nodes[].attributes.schema`, `defaults.attributes.by_executor.<executor>.<key>`. HTTP routes `GET /v1/nodes/{id}`, `POST /v1/runs/{run_id}/attributes` (the supervisor's callback listener), `POST /v1/instances/{id}/debug/override`. Event kinds `attributes_substituted`, `attributes_committed`, `attributes_schema_failed`, `attribute_override_matched`. Error class `attributes_schema_failed`. Signal `attribute/<key>/changed`.

Overrides come in layers, and they are not symmetrical between the two levels. At the template level `defaults.attributes` takes `by_executor` only; `by_node` and `by_match` are refused at YAML parse. At the instance level the create request's overrides take all three.

**node-subscription** (alias: subscription) — A per-node declaration of what wakes it: a signal type-path (exact or trailing-`*`), an optional `when:` CEL predicate over the signal payload, an optional sender-node filter, and a required `force_upstream_refresh` boolean. Only the three cascade-firing signals are subscribable — `terminal/success`, `terminal/error/<class>`, and `attribute/<key>/changed`. A subscription is also a wake declaration: there is no way to read a sender's data without also being woken by it. Every substitution reference in a node's schema must be covered by a subscription, or registration refuses the template.

*Where you meet it:* Template keys `nodes[].subscribes[].node`, `.type`, `.when`, `.force_upstream_refresh`. The fourth key on that entry, `nodes[].subscribes[].resolves_via_calling_node`, is set by canonicalization and rejected if you declare it.

**message-schema** — The template-level registry of message types an instance accepts. Each entry pairs a type-path with a JSON Schema body shape. An instance sent an undeclared type refuses the request.

*Where you meet it:* Template keys `messages[].type`, `messages[].body_schema`.

**message-sender-node** — A node whose dispatch mode is "build a message envelope from my attributes and post it." You declare it with `nodes[].sends_message: <type>` in place of an executor or a delegate. It uses the ordinary subscription and attribute machinery, so aggregating several upstreams into one message body needs no new primitive. Its attribute schema must match the destination type's body schema exactly.

*Where you meet it:* Template key `nodes[].sends_message`. Event kind `message_sent`.

**error-policy** (alias: error-types policy chain) — The per-node map from error class to one of four runtime actions: `pass`, `give_up`, `retry`, `release_and_requeue`. `nodes[].max_retries` bounds the total retries in one dispatch; exhausting it settles the run as failed. Both executor-emitted failures and rimsky's own acquisition failures route through the same map. With no matching entry, rimsky gives up — fail-fast is the default and retry is opt-in.

*Where you meet it:* Template keys `nodes[].error_types.<class>.action`, `nodes[].error_types.<class>.reason`, `nodes[].max_retries`, `nodes[].retry_backoff.kind|jitter|base_delay_ms|max_delay_ms`. Signals `transient/retry/<n>/<class>`, `transient/release_and_requeue/<class>`, `transient/infra/<class>`.

Write the exact class name. A bare `*` entry and a `<prefix>/*` entry both register — with a warning that the class is in no declared vocabulary — and then route nothing, so a node relying on either fails as though it had no policy at all. Only three of the eight per-node timing and retry keys have a deployment-wide default under `dispatch_defaults`; `max_retries` and the four `retry_backoff` subkeys are per-node only, and writing them under `dispatch_defaults` stops the deployment at startup.

**cascade-mode** — A per-node setting choosing what happens when a second cascade round targets a node that already has a pending or recently-settled run in the same scope. Four values: `most-recent` (the default: drop the earlier round), `sequenced` (queue both, so every round dispatches), `idempotent-queue` (drop a round whose bag duplicates a queued one), and `idempotent-settled` (also dedupe against the most recently settled run).

*Where you meet it:* Template key `nodes[].cascade_mode`.

**named-lock** — A producer-independent capacity counter, declared in operator config with one limit per name. A limit of one is a mutex; a higher limit is a counting semaphore. A node takes one by name; at runtime it becomes a row in the claim-handle ledger.

*Where you meet it:* Config key `named_locks.<name>.limit`. Template key `nodes[].locks[].name`. Event kinds `lock_acquired`, `lock_released`, `lock_orphan_reaped`.

## Execution: instances, frames, and cascade

**instance** — One live deployment of a template, identified by a rimsky-generated UUID and bound to a specific template hash. You create it with params and optional attribute overrides. Creation makes the instance and its node rows and fires the instance-created lifecycle callback; nothing runs until a sender posts a message. The instance owns the message queue that accumulates wakes while a frame is in flight, and its `message_queue_mode` — `backlog` (the default, keeping every wake) or `coalesce` (keeping the newest).

*Where you meet it:* CLI verbs `rimsky instance create|list|get|status|delete|kill|nodes|events`, and the shorthands `rimsky instantiate|rm-instance|ls instances|watch|logs`. HTTP routes `POST /v1/instances`, `GET /v1/instances`, `GET /v1/instances/{idOrKey}`, `POST /v1/instances/{idOrKey}/pause|resume|terminate`, `DELETE /v1/instances/{idOrKey}`, `GET /v1/instances/{id}/frames`, `GET /v1/instances/{id}/messages`. MCP tools `instance_create`, `instance_list`, `instance_get`, `instance_pause`, `instance_resume`, `instance_terminate`, `instance_kill`, `instance_frame_list`, `instance_frame_get`. Permission actions `instance:read|create|terminate|pause|resume|kill|list-frames|read-frame|debug-override`. Event kind `instance_terminated`. Template key `message_queue_mode`.

Creating an instance under a key you have used before is idempotent — the second call returns the same instance id. Two details bite when scripting. First, the identifier a route accepts follows the route's own spelling: the nine `{idOrKey}` routes take either the UUID or your instance key, and the ten `{id}` routes — assets, frames, messages, debug override — reject the key with 400. Second, pause and resume exist only over HTTP and MCP; `rimsky instance pause` is not a command.

**message** — A typed envelope whose arrival enqueues on an instance's message queue. The frame engine picks one message up and opens the next frame with it — one message per frame. The envelope's type selects an entry from the template's message-schema registry, and an undeclared type is refused at receipt. The envelope carries an identity, the target instance, the typed body, a receipt timestamp, and a sender-kind discriminator naming one of three origins: operator, publisher, or instance. Every declared type — plus the runtime's implicit empty type — materializes a message-receiver node at instance creation, which is what subscribers subscribe to.

*Where you meet it:* CLI verbs `rimsky messages tail|show`. HTTP routes `POST /v1/instances/{id}/messages`, `GET /v1/instances/{id}/messages`, `GET /v1/messages/{id}`. MCP tools `message_send`, `message_list`, `message_get`. Permission actions `message:send`, `message:read`. CLI flags `--message-type`, `--sender-kind`. Event kinds `message_received`, `message_sent`, `message.dead_lettered`. Config key `retention.message_idempotencies_trailing`.

Sending an empty message is the universal way to wake every structural root without crafting a typed envelope.

**frame** (alias: cascade-frame) — One cascade resolution. A frame begins when the frame engine picks a message off the queue, and ends when every run in it reaches a terminal state. Its lifecycle value is `running`, `completed` (quiescence reached), `failed` (the cascade broke), or `terminated` (administrative termination interrupted it). Frames are serial per instance: at most one runs at a time, and new messages accumulate on the queue behind it. Frames are isolated from one another — a running frame reads only its own triggering message and what its own work produced. The one carrier between frames is a message.

*Where you meet it:* HTTP routes `GET /v1/instances/{id}/frames`, `GET /v1/instances/{id}/frames/{frame_id}`, `GET /v1/observability/frames`, `GET /v1/observability/frames/{id}`, `GET /v1/admin/diagnostics/held-frames`. MCP tools `instance_frame_list`, `instance_frame_get`, `held_frames_list`. Permission actions `instance:list-frames`, `instance:read-frame`. Config keys `retention.recent_frames_kept`, `retention.trace_trailing`.

Ordering is per instance, not per template: two instances of one template run independently.

**run-scope** — The execution context for one graph instantiation inside a frame. Three kinds: the frame's root scope, a sub-graph scope, and a fan-out partition scope. Scopes form a tree through their parent pointer, rooted at the frame's root scope, and each owns a set of node-runs. Walking from a leaf scope to the root recovers the execution stack for that frame. A scope never spans frames.

*Where you meet it:* gRPC RPC `LifecycleSubscriber.OnRunScopeTerminal`. HTTP route `GET /v1/runs/{run_id}`. MCP tool `run_get`. Permission action `run:read`.

**node-run** — One execution of one node within a frame. Its state machine is a single seven-value column: `pending`, `stale`, `running`, `held`, `parked`, `fresh`, `failed`. The first five are in-flight and hold the frame open; `fresh` and `failed` are terminal. The row carries the frame and run-scope it belongs to, a progress timestamp for liveness, the executor's opaque scratch bytes, a link to the dispatch it supersedes with a reason (stale-recovery, retry-after-error, or recalculate), and a creation reason drawn from `cascade`, `operator_invalidate`, `recalculate`, `message_delivery`. Per-node attributes hang off this row.

*Where you meet it:* HTTP routes `GET /v1/runs/{run_id}`, `GET /v1/observability/node-runs`, `GET /v1/observability/node-runs/{id}`, `POST /v1/runs/{run_id}/keepalive`, `POST /v1/runs/{run_id}/attributes`. Event kinds `state_transition`, `work_started`, `work_completed`, `work_rejected`. MCP tool `run_get`.

**cascade** (alias: reactive-cascade) — The engine that turns one node-state transition into the downstream transitions it implies. It has one walk and two node-level behaviors. **Propagation** marks dependents stale on a subscription-edge match whose `when:` predicate holds, inserts wait-set rows, and recurses. **Fallthrough** rolls a node with no executor forward without running it. The walk is event-driven: it fires inside the transaction that settles the triggering signal, not as a separate ordered pass.

*Where you meet it:* HTTP route `GET /v1/observability/instances/{id}`, whose response carries the instance's cascade graph — its nodes joined with their subscription edges, each node's run summary, and its last terminal event. Event kinds `subgraph_internal_cascade_fired`, `fan_out_dispatched`. Transition reason `pure_cascade`, carried in the `state_transition` payload.

**wait-set** — The per-frame ledger recording "this receiver is waiting for this sender in this frame." Cascade walks insert rows; when a sender settles, rimsky stamps the matching rows drained and runs the gate evaluator for each waiting receiver. The gate evaluator advances a receiver from `pending` to `stale` only when its rows are all drained, no subscribed upstream is still in flight in the frame, and no other run for the same node and scope is already past pending. It then builds the receiver's attribute bag and applies the node's cascade mode. The dispatcher claims `stale` rows; it no longer checks dependencies.

*Where you meet it:* HTTP route `GET /v1/admin/diagnostics/wait-sets`. MCP tool `waitset_list`. Permission action `waitset:read`.

**signal** — The unified emission shape for any transition that affects a node-run: a canonical type-path plus a typed payload. The taxonomy is closed — `terminal/success`, `terminal/error/*`, `attribute/*/changed`, `transient/park`, `transient/await_async`, `transient/retry/*`, `transient/infra/*`, `transient/release_and_requeue/*`. Only the `terminal/*` and `attribute/*` kinds fire cascade; the `transient/*` family is audit-only, and subscribing to one is rejected at registration. Every signal writes one row to the event feed with its type-path as the kind — that is the only place the payload is durably kept. Subscribers receive the wake, not the payload.

*Where you meet it:* Template key `nodes[].subscribes[].type`. Event kinds — the signal type-paths appear alongside the 44 operational kinds in `GET /v1/events`.

**transition-reason** — The closed vocabulary explaining why a node-state transition happened: `gate_cleared`, `dispatch_claimed`, `policy_give_up`, `pure_cascade`, `dispatch_impossible`, `acquire_pass`, `handler_complete`, `handler_held`, `handler_pass`, `handler_park`, `fanout_dispatched`, `auto_terminal_commit`, `auto_terminal_abandon`, `deadline_resume`, `cascade_resume`, `child_transitioned`, `subgraph_internal_cascade_fired`, `instance_killed`, `sibling_cancelled`. Rimsky's state machine switches on (current state, reason) and rejects illegal sequences. The reason is never an event kind of its own.

*Where you meet it:* The `reason` field in the payload of a `state_transition` event row.

**terminal-tag** — A string in the tag set an executor attaches to a settling verdict. Tags are a per-emission label: they ride the event row and the subscriber's CEL evaluation, and they never merge into attribute state. Rimsky checks every tag against the emitting executor's advertised tag set, both when you register a subscription referencing a tag literal and when a verdict carries one at runtime. Unrelated to a template tag.

*Where you meet it:* Template key `nodes[].subscribes[].when` (predicating over `payload.tags`). Executor attribute key `http-node: stub_tags`.

**parked-state** (aliases: park, parked node) — One of the seven node-run states, entered from `running` when an executor emits a park outcome. A parked node is neither running nor failed. It carries a required resume-at timestamp, the executor's opaque scratch bytes, and tags. Two things wake it: the clock at resume-at, and a cascade event from a subscribed upstream. Both transition it to `stale` and re-dispatch the same row with the same attribute bag it saw originally — no substitution rebuild. Executors thread their own state across a park through scratch. Park is dispatch-internal: it ends a dispatch but not a run, writes no attributes, and never fires cascade.

*Where you meet it:* CLI verb `rimsky parked list`. CLI flag `--older-than`. HTTP route `GET /v1/admin/diagnostics/parked-nodes`. MCP tool `parked_node_list`. Permission action `parked-node:read`. Signal `transient/park`. Event kind `parked_resume_started`. Executor attribute keys `http-node: probe_park`, `http-node: park_resume_at`.

Parking is an executor's behavior, not a platform-level attribute family. `probe_park` and `park_resume_at` register on any node's schema, but only two of the four bundled executors act on them: `http-node` and `claude-agent` park; `verifier-http` completes normally and `verifier-shape-checks` errors.

**terminal-resolution** (alias: executor-terminal-spine) — The spine that takes one executor outcome off the wire and converges it on four decisions: which signal type-path to emit, whether the run settles or retries in place, which producer verb to fire on each acquired claim, and when to delete the claim-handle rows. The wire carries four outcome variants — success, error, park, and await-async-callback — and rimsky adds a fifth internal kind, infra, for a violated contract. Producer verbs go to a durable per-producer outbox rather than being dialed inside the settlement transaction: the disposition is recorded first, the verb is delivered afterwards with retry and backoff, in order per producer and claim scope, and cascade never waits on a producer's acknowledgement.

*Where you meet it:* HTTP route `GET /v1/admin/diagnostics/producer-outbox`. Event kinds `claim_resolution.commit`, `claim_resolution.abandon`, `no_op_commit`, `error`. Error classes `executor_sync_timeout`, `executor_protocol_violation`, `abandoned`.

**child-execution** — The umbrella for the two mechanisms by which a parent run dispatches work into child contexts: fan-out and sub-graph delegation. They share a thin dispatch helper that creates child scopes and child runs from a partitions-by-children matrix, and nothing else. Each has its own settle primitive. **Carry** is delegation's: it fires once when the sub-graph's exit terminates, copies the exit's writeback onto the calling node, and closes the child context. **Aggregate** is fan-out's: it fires per clone, records each outcome on the parent claim handle, and computes the aggregate verdict once nothing is active.

*Where you meet it:* Event kinds `fanout.children_created`, `subgraph.dispatched`, `subgraph.exit_carry`.

**fan-out** — Cloning the calling node N times, one clone per partition, each in its own child scope. The producer decides N: rimsky hands it the parent claim and a partition request, and it returns sub-scope descriptors. There is no attribute aggregation across clones — fan-in happens at the claim-handle level under an aggregation policy you choose from four values: `strict`, `threshold`, `best_effort`, `first`.

*Where you meet it:* Template keys `nodes[].fan_out.claim`, `.partition_request`, `.parallelism`, `.error_policy.kind`, `.error_policy.max_failures`. gRPC RPC `ClaimProducer.SplitScope`. Event kinds `fan_out_dispatched`, `fanout.children_created`, `subclaim.acquired`. Substitution source `{{child.partition_key}}`.

**delegation** — Invoking a named sub-graph from a node by declaring `delegate:` instead of `executor:`. The calling node absorbs the sub-graph's entry and dispatches with the entry's executor; the sub-graph's other nodes run in a child scope. Delegation has no aggregation policy — the settle primitive follows from the dispatch path, not from configuration. A fan-out clone may itself delegate: N partitions produce N independent sub-graph invocations, each carrying up its own exit.

*Where you meet it:* Template key `nodes[].delegate`. Event kinds `subgraph.dispatched`, `subgraph.exit_carry`, `subgraph_internal_cascade_fired`.

**cancel-siblings** — What "fail fast" means under the `strict` aggregation policy. When one sub-claim abandons under a strict parent, rimsky walks the parent's other in-flight sub-claims and force-abandons each. It is intrinsic to strict, not a separate switch. A workflow that wants survivors picks a different policy — a `threshold` set to the full child count tolerates any number of failures short of total loss without triggering the walk.

*Where you meet it:* Template key `nodes[].fan_out.error_policy.kind`. Transition reason `sibling_cancelled`.

---

## Claims, locks, and data

**claim** — A node's request for access to a producer-managed resource: a table row, a filesystem path, a queue head, a snapshot. You declare it in `claims:` with a producer name, a selector, and an intent (`read` or `read_write`). At runtime the producer's open verb returns an address, a payload, a claim scope, and a realized write-semantics value — or reports the claim unavailable. Intent's only consumer is the coexistence predicate. Claims carry three orthogonal extensions: a lifetime, sub-claim chains from partitioning, and co-holdership.

*Where you meet it:* Template keys `nodes[].claim_producers[].name|selector|intent|alias|lifetime|data`. Substitution sources `{{claim.<alias>.address}}`, `{{claim.<alias>.claim_scope}}`, `{{claim.<alias>.payload...}}`. gRPC RPCs `ClaimProducer.Open|Commit|Abandon|Release`. Event kinds `claim_acquired`, `claim_held`, `claim_resolved`.

**claim-handle** — Rimsky's own ledger row for one acquired claim or named-lock acquisition: the lock identity, the acquired scope, an expiry and held marker, the realized write semantics, and a link back to the holding run. It also carries a parent pointer for sub-claims, fan-out counters, the lifetime selector, and the version the producer reported at commit. Its state is one of three: `active` (a supervisor holds it), `committed`, or `abandoned`. Transitions are guarded on the holding supervisor, and a settled row never returns to active. The handle is the single answer to "who holds what right now."

*Where you meet it:* HTTP routes `GET /v1/claim-handles/{claim_handle_id}/holders`, `GET /v1/observability/claim-handles`, `GET /v1/observability/claim-handles/{id}`. MCP tool `claim_holders_list`. Permission action `claim-holders:read`. Config key `retention.claim_handles_trailing`.

**claim-scope** — The opaque bytes a producer returns to identify what it acquired. Rimsky's default conflict predicate is byte-equality over those bytes; a producer that advertises the scopes-conflict capability supplies its own overlap predicate and rimsky asks it instead. Do not confuse the scope with the selector: the **selector** is the text you write in the template, which may still carry substitution directives at authoring time; the **claim scope** is what the producer commits to after resolving it. Scopes never contain directives.

*Where you meet it:* Template key `nodes[].claim_producers[].selector`. Substitution source `{{claim.<alias>.claim_scope}}`. gRPC RPC `ClaimProducer.ScopesConflict`.

**claim-producer** (alias: claim-store) — An implementation of the claim-producer protocol: four verbs — open, commit, abandon, release — plus capability advertisement. It runs out of process over gRPC, or in process inside the all-in-one binary; both go through the same protocol surface. Two optional methods sit on the service behind their own capability flags: split-scope (partitioning a scope for fan-out) and scopes-conflict (a producer-aware overlap predicate). Two further mix-ins are sibling protocols advertised in the capabilities list: validation and data-processing. A producer knows what "the same data" means in its own domain; rimsky does not.

*Where you meet it:* Config keys `claim_producers.<name>.endpoint|tls|protocols|write_semantics_allowed|observability_endpoint`. Compose manifest keys `claim_producers.<name>.*`. Proto files `claim_producer.proto`, `claim_producer_observability.proto`. gRPC RPCs `ClaimProducer.Capabilities|Open|Commit|Abandon|Release|SplitScope|ScopesConflict`. CLI verb `rimsky conformance claim-producer`. Images `rimsky-claim-producer-filesystem`, `rimsky-claim-producer-postgres`. Service config keys under `claim-producer-filesystem:` and `claim-producer-postgres:`.

**claim-lifetime** — A per-claim choice between `subgraph` (the default) and `durable`. Under both, the auto-terminal mechanism fires commit or abandon at the end of the holding subgraph. The difference is what happens to the row afterwards: a subgraph row is reaped by the retention sweep after its trailing window; a committed durable row is exempt, stays available for later dispatches to co-hold and for asset queries, and is released only by an explicit operator action or by deleting the instance.

*Where you meet it:* Template key `nodes[].claim_producers[].lifetime`. HTTP route `DELETE /v1/instances/{id}/assets/{alias}`. Config key `retention.claim_handles_trailing`.

**claim-co-holdership** — Several runs holding the same claim handle, declared with `holds:`. A co-holder adds a row against an existing handle rather than opening a new one, and the claim stays open until every co-holder is done. It supports claim-pass — a downstream node consuming the live claim's address, scope, and payload — as against value-pass, where a node copies fields into its own attributes and downstream nodes read those. The `from:` reference must name a node that acquired the alias in its own `claims:` block; co-holdership does not chain.

*Where you meet it:* Template keys `nodes[].holds.<alias>.from`, `nodes[].holds.<alias>.as`. Substitution source `{{claim.<alias>....}}` over the co-held alias. HTTP route `GET /v1/claim-handles/{claim_handle_id}/holders`.

**claim-tree** — The tree over claim-handle rows formed by the parent pointer. A root claim has none; a sub-claim points at its parent. Fan-out creates it: the producer returns N sub-scopes and rimsky inserts N child rows in the acquisition transaction. When a child resolves, rimsky walks up — and only once every holder and every child on the parent is settled does it compute the parent's aggregate verdict and fire the parent's own terminal.

*Where you meet it:* HTTP routes `GET /v1/lineage/claims/{claim_handle_id}/ancestors`, `.../descendants`. MCP tools `lineage_claim_ancestors`, `lineage_claim_descendants`. Event kind `subclaim.acquired`.

**write-semantics** — A four-value per-claim enum deciding how the coexistence matrix treats concurrent claims on the same scope. The producer advertises what it supports, the operator narrows that per producer in config, and each open returns the one realized value. `sync` is in-place with no staging: readers coexist, and anything involving a writer conflicts. `staged_async` stages writes and shows readers the pre-stage snapshot: only writer-writer conflicts. `blocking_async` stages writes but blocks readers, so its verdict matches `sync`. `read_only` rejects writes at open, so only reader-reader is reachable.

*Where you meet it:* Config key `claim_producers.<name>.write_semantics_allowed`. Compose manifest key `claim_producers.<name>.write_semantics_allowed`. Service config key `claim-producer-postgres: write_semantics`.

**atomic-staging** — The producer-side discipline that realizes staged-asynchronous writes: writers stage into a side area, commit swaps it into the canonical view, abandon drops it. Readers see the pre-stage snapshot until the swap lands. It composes with subgraph-lifetime claims and co-holding verifier nodes — the verifiers' terminals feed the aggregation that decides commit or abandon. Rimsky does not interpret the substrate; the atomicity is the producer's to provide.

*Where you meet it:* gRPC RPCs `ClaimProducer.Commit`, `ClaimProducer.Abandon`. Service config key `claim-producer-filesystem: pick_policies.<name>.sync_strategy`.

**auto-terminal** (alias: held-claim resolution) — The mechanism that fires a producer's commit or abandon exactly once at the end of a held claim's holding subgraph. It waits until every expected holder has recorded itself and every expected fan-out child has resolved, computes the aggregate outcome, enqueues the verb on the outbox, and promotes the handle row — all in the settlement transaction. It is also the deferred cascade moment: on commit, held holders go `held → fresh` and `terminal/success` fires downstream; on abandon they go `held → failed` and `terminal/error/abandoned` fires.

*Where you meet it:* Event kinds `claim_resolution.commit`, `claim_resolution.abandon`, `claim_held`, `claim_resolved`. Error class `abandoned`. Transition reasons `auto_terminal_commit`, `auto_terminal_abandon`.

**data-processing** — An optional mix-in protocol on a claim producer, advertised by listing it in the capabilities handshake. It carries the control plane for a typed-data version lifecycle: begin, commit, and abandon a candidate, plus reads for version history, partition manifests, and per-version schema. Data motion stays substrate-direct through the acquired claim's address; the protocol carries no bytes.

*Where you meet it:* Proto file `data_processing.proto`. gRPC RPCs `DataProcessing.Capabilities|BeginCandidate|CommitCandidate|AbandonCandidate|ListVersions|ListPartitions|GetVersionSchema`. CLI verb `rimsky conformance data-processing`. Config keys `data_processors.<name>.endpoint|tls|protocols|observability_endpoint`. Event kind `subclaim.begin_candidate`.

**asset** — Not a new primitive: a committed claim with a durable lifetime against a producer that advertises data-processing. Anything satisfying all three is an asset; anything else is not. Rimsky surfaces assets by querying claim handles matching that description.

*Where you meet it:* CLI verbs `rimsky asset list|show|versions|delete|lineage`. HTTP routes `GET /v1/instances/{id}/assets`, `GET /v1/instances/{id}/assets/{alias}`, `.../versions`, `.../materialization-history`, `DELETE /v1/instances/{id}/assets/{alias}`. MCP tools `asset_list`, `asset_get`, `asset_versions`, `asset_materialization_history`, `asset_delete`. Permission actions `asset:read`, `asset:delete`. Template key `nodes[].claim_producers[].lifetime: durable`.

One asset operation is CLI-only: `rimsky asset lineage` has no matching route and no matching MCP tool. Re-materializing an asset is expressed by sending the instance a message, not by an asset verb.

**lineage** — A persisted projection of what each run's output depended on and what each claim handle resolved to. Two append-only record kinds. Rimsky writes the projection forward at terminal time from the event log and the claim-handle lifecycle; it does not reconstruct it on demand. Lineage does not capture wake-only causality — a consumer woken by an upstream whose attributes it never read. For that, read the event feed's signal rows or the wait-set ledger.

*Where you meet it:* CLI verbs `rimsky lineage prune`, `rimsky asset lineage`. HTTP routes `GET /v1/lineage/runs/{run_id}`, `.../ancestors`, `.../descendants`, `GET /v1/lineage/claims/{claim_handle_id}`, `.../ancestors`, `.../descendants`, `GET /v1/lineage/by-producer/{executor_name}`, `GET /v1/lineage/by-source/{source_type}/{source_id}`, `POST /v1/admin/lineage/prune`. MCP tools `lineage_get`, `lineage_run_ancestors`, `lineage_run_descendants`, `lineage_claim_ancestors`, `lineage_claim_descendants`, `lineage_prune`. Permission actions `lineage:read`, `lineage:prune`. Config key `retention.lineage_trailing`. Image `rimsky-subscriber-openlineage`.

**lineage-record** — One row in that projection. A **leaf-run record** captures the computational unit: which run terminated, where it sat in the run tree, what triggered its frame, what it substituted from upstream, what claims it held, and how it ended. A **claim-terminal record** captures the data-promotion unit: which handle resolved, its place in the claim tree, the producer, the substrate identity, and the disposition. The projection covers every claim-handle terminal, so commits and both flavors of abandon are all reconstructable.

*Where you meet it:* The lineage routes and MCP tools above return these two record kinds.

---

## Services and protocols

**service** — Any implementation of one or more rimsky protocols that rimsky orchestrates, running as an out-of-process binary or as an in-process handler inside the all-in-one process. Both forms dispatch through the same protocol surface. A binary implementing N protocols uses N distinct handlers registered separately — protocols are never collapsed into one.

*Where you meet it:* Config keys `executors.<name>.protocols`, `claim_producers.<name>.protocols`, `publishers.<name>.protocols`, `validators.<name>.protocols`, `data_processors.<name>.protocols`. Compose manifest keys of the same shape. Bundled services: `claude-agent`, `http-node`, `verifier-http`, `verifier-shape-checks`, `claim-producer-filesystem`, `claim-producer-postgres`, `sensor-cron`, `sensor-http`, `sensor-object-store`, `sensor-webhook`, `openlineage`.

Two expectations to set aside when operating the bundle. Only two listeners in the whole shipped set answer `GET /health` — the supervisor's callback listener and `sensor-webhook`'s HTTP ingress; the control API answers at `/v1/health` instead. And no bundled service exposes Prometheus metrics; the metrics ports belong to the three core roles only.

**executor** — An implementation of the executor protocol's unary execute call, plus an optional observability protocol. It receives one request and returns exactly one outcome: success, error, park, or a deferral to an async callback. Out-of-process executors give language portability and long-running work; in-process handlers give utility primitives without the deploy and IPC overhead. Executors own their per-dispatch work, their outcome, and their opaque scratch bytes. Rimsky owns dispatch routing, substitution, schema validation, and what to do with an error.

*Where you meet it:* Template key `nodes[].executor`. Config keys `executors.<name>.transport|endpoint|tls|protocols|observability_endpoint`. Proto files `executor.proto`, `executor_observability.proto`. gRPC RPCs `Executor.Execute`, `ExecutorObservability.Capabilities|GetTrace|StreamTrace`. CLI verbs `rimsky conformance executor`, `rimsky conformance probe`. Images `rimsky-executor-http-node`, `rimsky-executor-verifier-http`, `rimsky-executor-verifier-shape-checks`, `rimsky-executor-claude-agent`. Executor attribute keys under `claude-agent:`, `http-node:`, `verifier-http:`, `verifier-shape-checks:`. Error classes `agent/*`, `http/*`, `verifier/*`, `spawn_failed`. Environment variables `RIMSKY_EXECUTOR_*`.

Three things about the executor surface differ from what its shape suggests. `Executor.Execute` has no `Capabilities` RPC — an executor advertises through the observability protocol instead. The error-class catalog is not a versioned vocabulary: it is whatever the services configured at your deployment advertise, and the handshake carries no version or deprecation marker. And `stub_response` is honored differently per bundled executor: `http-node` returns your object, `claude-agent` returns it only when the node also sets `stub_probe`, and the two verifiers ignore it.

**publisher** — A service that publishes messages into rimsky. It implements four verbs — capabilities, subscribe, unsubscribe, list-subscriptions — and POSTs envelopes to the universal message-send route, identifying itself as a publisher and presenting a per-subscription capability token. One publisher process serves many instances: each subscription provisions a logical per-instance broadcaster parameterized by that instance's resolved config.

*Where you meet it:* Template keys `publishers[].name|kind|config|message_type`. Config keys `publishers.<name>.endpoint|tls|protocols|observability_endpoint`. Proto file `publisher.proto`. gRPC RPCs `Publisher.Capabilities|Subscribe|Unsubscribe|ListSubscriptions`. CLI verb `rimsky conformance publisher`. HTTP route `POST /v1/instances/{id}/messages`.

**sensor** — The class of publisher that watches external state — a clock, an HTTP endpoint, an object-store prefix, a webhook port — and publishes a message when the watched thing changes. Four kinds ship: `cron`, `http`, `object-store`, `webhook`. Each holds its own per-subscription state (next fire time, body hash, watermark cursor, last idempotency key) in its own database.

*Where you meet it:* Template key `publishers[].kind`. Publisher config keys `cron: cron`; `http: url|poll_interval|match.status|match.jsonpath.path|match.jsonpath.value`; `object-store: backend|bucket|prefix|poll_interval|settle_window|watermark_field`; `webhook: path_prefix|idempotency_header|auth.mode|auth.secret|auth.signature_header|auth.timestamp_header|auth.replay_window_seconds|auth.header`. Images `rimsky-sensor-cron`, `rimsky-sensor-http`, `rimsky-sensor-object-store`, `rimsky-sensor-webhook`. HTTP routes `POST /{path_prefix}/*` and `GET /health` on the webhook ingress. Environment variables `RIMSKY_SENSOR_*`.

Two sensor keys mean less than their names suggest. `object-store: backend` names a local backend, not a cloud one: the build serves `filesystem` and `memory`, and a publisher declaring `s3`, `gcs`, or `azure` stays in `mounting` and never goes active. And the `auth:` block is webhook-only in effect: an `http` publisher accepts it at registration and deploy, mounts live, and then polls its upstream without presenting the credential.

**publisher-subscription** (alias: sensor-watch) — The rimsky-side binding for one instance, publisher, and message type. Rimsky creates it at instance creation from the template's `publishers:` entry, tracks its state — `mounting`, `active`, `failed`, `stopped` — with a failure reason where it failed, and reconciles the publisher toward it. The row set is desired state, so a reconciliation worker drives unmounted rows toward active and a startup pass re-drives rows the publisher dropped. The instance read exposes per-subscription state, so you can watch mounting progress rather than infer it.

*Where you meet it:* HTTP route `GET /v1/instances/{idOrKey}`. Template keys `publishers[].*`.

**lifecycle-subscriber** — A service that opts into control-plane notifications by declaring the lifecycle-subscriber protocol alongside its primary one. Seven callbacks: template registered, deployed, undeployed, deregistered; instance created and terminated; and run-scope terminal. It carries the control-plane and instance lifecycle deliberately and not node-cascade events — a subscriber that needs node-level transitions reads the event feed instead. Rimsky stages each delivery in the transaction that performs the transition and drains it in order per service and per object, so an event arrives at least once and a handler must be idempotent.

*Where you meet it:* Proto file `lifecycle.proto`. gRPC RPCs `LifecycleSubscriber.OnTemplateRegistered|OnTemplateDeployed|OnTemplateUndeployed|OnTemplateDeregistered|OnInstanceCreated|OnInstanceTerminated|OnRunScopeTerminal`. CLI verb `rimsky conformance lifecycle-subscriber`. Config key `<service>.protocols`. Service config keys `claim-producer-filesystem: enable_lifecycle`, `claim-producer-postgres: enable_lifecycle`. Image `rimsky-subscriber-openlineage`.

**validation** — A cross-cutting protocol any service may advertise. It has one method. The request names the role whose registration it validates and carries exactly one role-specific context; the response is a valid/invalid flag plus errors and warnings. Rimsky calls it at template registration, giving each service a say in whether a node's attributes and bindings make sense in its domain. There is no runtime per-call validation.

*Where you meet it:* Proto file `validation.proto`. gRPC RPC `Validation.Validate`. CLI verb `rimsky conformance validation`. CLI flag `--role`. Config keys `validators.<name>.endpoint|tls|protocols|observability_endpoint`, `unreachable_validator_policy`. HTTP route `POST /v1/templates/validate`. Permission action `template:validate`.

**observability** — The two optional service-facing observability protocols and the startup handshake that probes them: executor-observability, exposing a capabilities query plus single-trace fetch and trace streaming, and claim-producer-observability, exposing capabilities, claim detail, claim-state streaming, claim-inventory pagination, and producer-declared admin views. A service implements at most one, matching its kind. The handshake also carries the executor's expected-attributes schema, which rimsky applies at registration and at dispatch.

*Where you meet it:* Config key `<service>.observability_endpoint`. gRPC RPCs `ExecutorObservability.*`, `ClaimProducerObservability.*`. HTTP routes `GET /v1/observability/executors`, `GET /v1/observability/executors/{name}`, `GET /v1/observability/claim-producers`, `GET /v1/observability/claim-producers/{name}`. CLI flag `--check-observability`. Environment variable `RIMSKY_OBSERVABILITY_REFRESH_INTERVAL`. Error class `executor_schema_unavailable`. Event kind `executor_schema_unavailable`.

Only two service classes have an observability sibling. A stack accepts `observability_endpoint` on a publisher or a validator and starts healthy, but no protocol answers behind it and no route reads it.

**discovery-cache** (alias: capabilities cache) — The in-memory cache of what each service advertises, filled by the startup handshake for out-of-process services and by registration for in-process handlers. It holds two indexes, one per service kind, each keyed by service name. An entry carries the service's declared tags, declared error classes, expected-attributes schema, observability availability, and reachability. Rimsky consults it at template registration — for the tag cross-check, the error-class check, and the schema gate — and at dispatch to resolve the schema, rather than probing the service each time.

*Where you meet it:* HTTP routes `GET /v1/observability/executors`, `GET /v1/observability/claim-producers`. Environment variable `RIMSKY_OBSERVABILITY_REFRESH_INTERVAL`.

**service-address-book** — The shared, persisted catalog mapping declared executor and claim-producer names to endpoints. The control plane publishes the deployment's declarations at startup and on reload; every supervisor resolves names against it read-through rather than against its own boot-time snapshot. Because every supervisor can resolve every name, a queued run never waits unclaimable — a name that resolves nowhere fails inside a claimed dispatch, loudly, instead of stalling in the queue.

*Where you meet it:* Config keys `executors.<name>.endpoint`, `claim_producers.<name>.endpoint`. Error class `unresolved_executor`. Event kind `unresolved_executor`.

**conformance** — A per-protocol subcommand family over a shared library in the protocols module. A third-party implementer points a subcommand at their endpoint; a Go author can call the same library from a test. Seven subcommands ship: `executor`, `claim-producer`, `publisher`, `validation`, `data-processing`, `lifecycle-subscriber`, and `probe`.

*Where you meet it:* CLI verbs `rimsky conformance executor|claim-producer|publisher|validation|data-processing|lifecycle-subscriber|probe`. CLI flags `--endpoint`, `--transport`, `--scenarios`, `--skip`, `--allow-live`, `--check-observability`, `--retention-test-seconds`, `--callback-bind`, `--callback-host`, `--tls`, `--timeout`. Image `rimsky-conformance`.

One subcommand covers something other than a protocol, and two of the shipped protocols have no subcommand at all: nothing in the kit proves a host-daemon or an executor-observability implementation. For CI, note that no subcommand accepts `--json` or `--warnings-as-errors` — parse the printed `ok` / `FAIL` rows and the closing count — and that three exit codes cover every outcome, so "failed a check" and "could not reach the endpoint" are not separable by exit code alone.

**host-daemon** — A daemon on a developer's machine. It dials a host-daemon proxy outbound over TLS, verifying the proxy's certificate against a pinned deployment CA root, and authenticates inside that channel as the user — carrying the user's API key, or, with none configured, an anonymous routing identity. It then serves spawn, dispatch, and reap requests against local binaries and relays their callbacks. A spawned binary must read `RIMSKY_DAEMON_PORT` and bind its gRPC server there; there is no port handshake back.

*Where you meet it:* CLI verbs `rimsky daemon start|status|stop`. CLI flags `--proxy`, `--listen`, `--label`, `--identity-file`, `--allow-paths`, `--foreground`, `--api-key`, `--tls`, `--tls-ca`, `--service`. Binary `rimsky-host-daemon`. Environment variables `RIMSKY_DAEMON_*`, `RIMSKY_HOST_DAEMON_PROXY_URL`. Proto file `host_daemon.proto`. gRPC RPC `HostDaemon.Connect`. Template key `late_bind_services`. Error class `spawn_failed`.

**host-daemon-proxy** — The stack-side counterpart. It presents the ordinary rimsky service protocols to the supervisor, holds the long-lived daemon connections on the developer-facing side, and routes each dispatch to whichever daemon is connected under the instance's stamped routing identity. It rewrites callback URLs so spawned processes post to the daemon's local listener rather than dialing the supervisor. Declare it once per protocol it fronts, all entries pointing at the same binary.

*Where you meet it:* Binary `rimsky-host-daemon-proxy`. Image `rimsky-host-daemon-proxy`. Config keys `late_bind_service_proxies.<name>`, `executors.<name>.endpoint`. Environment variables `RIMSKY_PROXY_GRPC_PORT`, `RIMSKY_PROXY_SERVICE_GRPC_PORT`, `RIMSKY_PROXY_TLS_CERT`, `RIMSKY_PROXY_TLS_KEY`, `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_URL`, `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_TOKEN`, `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_CA`. Ports 8090 (daemon-facing) and 8091 (service-facing mTLS).

---

## Operating the platform

**control-api** — The operator interface. It serves two protocol skins on one TCP port over one operation set: a direct request/response REST surface for scripts and tooling, and an agentic tool surface whose catalog it computes from the canonical action registry and filters by the calling key's grant. Both skins pass through the same auth and permission middleware. It fires lifecycle-subscriber events at the state transitions it performs, and under mutual TLS it hosts the deployment CA and the enrollment endpoint.

*Where you meet it:* All 92 public HTTP routes under `/v1`. MCP methods `initialize`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`, `resources/list`, `resources/read`, over `POST /v1/mcp`, `GET /v1/mcp`, `DELETE /v1/mcp`. Binary `rimsky-control-api`. Image command `rimsky-control-api`. Port 8080. Permission actions `mcp:read`, `health:probe`, `auth:whoami`, `observability:read`. Environment variables `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_HOST`, `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_PORT`.

Some things a REST client should not assume here. The `/v1` prefix is a path literal, not a negotiable version: there is no discovery route and an unknown version answers the same plain 404 a misspelled path does. The error envelope is not uniform — four shapes come back across the surface, and the core families answer `{"error": "<human string>"}` with no machine-readable code. `GET /v1/events` has no streaming or follow mode; `Accept: text/event-stream` returns a complete finite JSON body. And no `DELETE` route is idempotent except `DELETE /v1/mcp`: the second delete answers 404.

The two skins nearly cover each other. The 57 MCP tools and the REST routes reach almost the same action set, with a handful of routes having no tool. The catalog filter holds for plain action-level grants: a read-only key sees only read tools. It does not account for scope — a tool gated by a scoped grant is listed even where the scope will refuse the call. The `rimsky://` resource scheme is exactly the two breakpoint-hit forms and nothing else, and the server implements exactly the five MCP methods above; other base-protocol methods answer `method not found`.

**cascade-graph** (alias: operator dashboard backplane) — The read-only route family the control API exposes for operators and dashboards: rimsky's own persisted runtime state, plus discovered service status from the capabilities cache. The per-instance read carries the concept's namesake — the instance's nodes joined with their subscription edges, each node's run summary, and its last terminal event.

*Where you meet it:* HTTP routes `GET /v1/observability/executors`, `/claim-producers`, `/templates`, `/instances`, `/frames`, `/nodes/{instance_id}/{node_type}`, `/node-runs`, `/claim-handles`, `/events`, `/system/health`, `/system/summary`, and their by-id forms. MCP tool `observability_get`. Permission action `observability:read`.

Read this family as a second surface, not a read-only mirror of the primary routes. The shapes differ: `GET /v1/instances/{id}` returns the instance at the top level, and `GET /v1/observability/instances/{id}` nests it beside the cascade graph. Its error envelope differs too.

**rimsky** (alias: rimsky-cli) — The operator CLI: a thin HTTP+JSON client over the control API. It also carries two embedded one-shot modes that self-host the whole stack without any rimsky infrastructure — `rimsky run` drives a single template to terminal, and `rimsky compose run` drives a manifest to terminal. The CLI resolves file references in spec YAML before submitting, expands bundled roles into grants client-side, and doubles as the host daemon under `rimsky daemon start`.

*Where you meet it:* 93 CLI verbs and 77 CLI flags. Config keys `~/.rimsky/config.yml: current_context|contexts.<name>.endpoint|contexts.<name>.api_key|aliases.<name>`. CLI verbs `rimsky ctx list|use|add|rm|current`. Environment variables `RIMSKY_CONTEXT`, `RIMSKY_API_KEY`, `RIMSKY_CONFIG`. Compose manifest keys `project`, `context`, `templates[].path|tag|state`, `instances[].template|name|params|restart`. Permission action `compose:origin`. Published packages: the four `rimsky_<version>_{linux,darwin}_{amd64,arm64}` release archives and `checksums.txt`.

The CLI's flag surface is less uniform than its size suggests, and the gaps are worth knowing before scripting:

- **`--json` is not global.** Exactly one verb accepts it — `rimsky auth list`. The other read verbs spell JSON output `-o json`, and the two spellings sit on disjoint verb sets, so on any given verb one of them is a parse error. `-o yaml` is rejected; `-o table` is accepted and silently means human-readable.
- **Short flags are not a family.** `-o` is a genuine short form of `--output`. `-f` is not a short form of `--follow` or `--force`; it is defined only in the compose family, where it names the manifest path.
- **`--help` exits 2 on a leaf verb.** The root and the family nodes — `rimsky template --help`, `rimsky auth --help` — exit 0; every leaf verb prints its usage to stderr and exits 2. A script treating a non-zero exit as failure will misread `rimsky conformance executor --help`.
- **Destructive verbs do not prompt.** Eleven destructive verbs ask nothing, on a terminal or otherwise, and `--yes` suppresses no prompt because there is none to suppress. On `rimsky instance kill` it stands in for `--force`, so it enables the destruction rather than confirming it. The compose family is the exception: `rimsky compose down` prints what it will destroy and asks. `rimsky instance kill` without `--force` also stops, by refusing rather than by asking.
- **Duration flags do not share one grammar.** Three grammars are in play across the duration-shaped flags and config keys.
- **Time-window flags are not uniform.** `--since`, `--until`, `--before`, and `--older-than` each reach a different small subset of the time-ordered reads. `rimsky messages tail` defines neither `--since` nor `--until`.
- **`--control-api` and `--api-key` are not the general endpoint flags.** The general spellings are `--endpoint` and `--key`, and even those are not universal — `ctx current`, `daemon status`, `daemon start`, and `compose run` take neither. `--control-api` and `--api-key` each appear on exactly one verb, meaning something specific there. The compose family is the case to watch: `rimsky compose status --endpoint <url> --key <key>` accepts both flags and then sends the request with no credential, and `RIMSKY_API_KEY` does not fill the gap, so `up`, `down`, `plan`, and `status` cannot authenticate against a deployment that has left anonymous mode.
- **There is no `--dry-run` flag.** The capability is real and lives on the HTTP surface as a `?dry_run=true` query parameter; no CLI write verb exposes it.

Two compose keys mean less than their names promise. `instances[].restart` supervises nothing — nothing re-creates a terminated instance under `restart: always`, and `compose status` reports the instance as in-manifest either way. And `templates[].state` is not fully declarative: `undeployed` is not an accepted value, so flipping the key refuses the manifest rather than undeploying anything.

**rimsky-yml** (alias: unified config) — One YAML file, read by every runtime process and by the migrate step, at a well-known default path. It declares persistence, named locks, retention, dispatch defaults, and one block per service protocol; each service entry may list which protocols that binary speaks. Decoding is strict: an unknown key fails the load with the offending key named. The unified entrypoint distinguishes only the process role — everything else is in this file.

*Where you meet it:* 57 config keys. Environment variable `RIMSKY_CONFIG`. Image path `/etc/rimsky/rimsky.yml`.

Configuration through the environment is narrower than the file. There is no general `RIMSKY_`-prefixed override for a config key: variables named the way an operator would guess — a persistence driver, a SQLite path, an executor endpoint — change nothing, and the deployment comes up on the file's values. The variables that do work are the named ones in the environment-variable class. And the strictness runs one way only: a misspelled YAML key stops the load with its name, while a misspelled `RIMSKY_*` variable is ignored silently and named nowhere in the startup log.

**api-key** (alias: bearer token) — A high-entropy, rimsky-issued credential carried as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. The server stores only a hash; the plaintext is surfaced once at mint and again at each rotation. The key ledger is rimsky's entire principal registry — there is no user entity, so a person is the holder of a key's plaintext and a service principal is an API key. Deployments needing richer identity terminate it at the edge and inject keys downstream.

*Where you meet it:* CLI verbs `rimsky auth init|login|create-key|list|show|revoke|rotate|status`. CLI flags `--key`, `--expires`, `--include-revoked`, `--key-prefix`, `--force-leave-anonymous`. HTTP routes `POST /v1/auth/keys`, `GET /v1/auth/keys`, `GET /v1/auth/keys/{nameOrID}`, `DELETE /v1/auth/keys/{nameOrID}`, `POST /v1/auth/keys/{nameOrID}/rotate`, `GET /v1/auth/status`, `GET /v1/auth/whoami`. MCP tools `auth_create_key`, `auth_list`, `auth_get`, `auth_revoke_key`, `auth_rotate_key`, `auth_status`. Permission actions `auth:read|create|revoke|rotate|whoami`. Event kinds `auth.key_created`, `auth.key_revoked`, `auth.key_rotated`, `auth.access_attempted`, `auth.access_denied`. Environment variable `RIMSKY_API_KEY`.

Capture the plaintext at mint. Neither `rimsky auth show` nor `GET /v1/auth/keys/{nameOrID}` returns it again — the read surfaces carry six fields and none is the key material. A key lapsing at its expiry also emits nothing: creation, rotation, and revocation each write an audit row, and expiry writes none, so a lapse is invisible in the feed.

**permission** (alias: grant, action) — The authorization grant attached to a key: a JSON array of entries, each pairing an action string with an optional mode (a dry-run floor) and an optional scope selector. Rimsky matches an action against a boundary-only wildcard grammar and evaluates the grant as set membership against the canonical action registry.

*Where you meet it:* 49 permission actions. HTTP route `POST /v1/auth/keys`. CLI flags `--role`, `--role-file`, `--add`, `--remove`. MCP tool `auth_create_key`.

The grammar is narrower than a glob. Three shapes are accepted — `*`, `<noun>:*`, and `*:<verb>` — and every infix or partial form (`instance:re*`, `inst*:read`, `*:re*`, `**`) is refused at key creation with the shapes it will take. The action registry is a closed list, not a CRUD matrix over nouns: `instance:update`, `asset:create`, `message:delete`, and sixteen similar guesses are each rejected as an unknown action. Scope is narrower still: it works on seven of the 46 grantable actions, all template- or tag-shaped, and the rest refuse a scope-bearing grant at key creation naming the action.

**role-template** (alias: bundled role) — A JSON resource compiled into the CLI that expands into a grant at key-creation time. Six ship: `admin`, `operator`, `read-only`, `agent-supervisor`, `publisher-service`, `debug-operator`. You can also pass a custom role as a local JSON file. The server has no notion of roles — it stores the expanded grant.

*Where you meet it:* Bundled roles `admin`, `agent-supervisor`, `debug-operator`, `operator`, `publisher-service`, `read-only`. CLI verb `rimsky auth create-key`. CLI flags `--role`, `--role-file`, `--add`, `--remove`.

Because expansion happens in the CLI, a role leaves no server-side trace. A key minted with `--role operator` reads back as its expanded grant entries, with nothing naming the role, and no route lists the roles.

**anonymous-mode** (alias: implicit anonymous mode) — A data-derived state, not a setting: while the key ledger has zero active rows, every credential-less request is admitted as a synthetic admin identity. A request that does present a credential is still validated normally, so a stale credential is rejected rather than silently promoted. The mode flips the moment the first key is minted. It exists to solve bootstrap — the first key gets minted through the same endpoint operators use afterwards.

*Where you meet it:* CLI verbs `rimsky auth init`, `rimsky auth status`. CLI flag `--force-leave-anonymous` on `rimsky auth revoke`. HTTP routes `GET /v1/auth/status`, `POST /v1/auth/keys`. MCP tool `auth_status`.

There is no configuration that turns anonymous mode off. Every plausible spelling of such a key — `anonymous_mode`, `auth.required`, `require_auth`, `auth_mode` — stops the deployment at startup as an unknown field. Minting the first key is what closes the window.

**dry-run** — Preview without commit. The resolved mode comes from a per-request flag or from an identity-bound grant mode, and the grant is a floor: a key whose matched entry is dry-run runs every covered write in dry-run, and the request flag cannot lift it. When a write resolves to dry-run, the handler validates — including side-effect-free calls out to the validation protocol — skips the mutation, and returns a preview envelope. The audit trail records the attempt as previewed.

*Where you meet it:* The `dry_run` query parameter on the control API's write routes. Permission grant entries carrying a mode. Event kinds `auth.access_attempted` (recording the resolved mode).

The capability is HTTP-side. No CLI write verb takes `--dry-run`, `--preview`, or `-n`.

**service-auth** (aliases: internal-service-auth, mtls) — The posture across rimsky's four trust boundaries, and the optional mutual-TLS mechanism for one of them. The boundaries are: the control plane, authenticated by API keys over TLS and acting as the identity authority the others defer to; internal service-to-service calls and their return legs; bundled-service ingress from the public web (the webhook sensor's port, the daemon-to-proxy hop), each with its own authentication; and outbound calls where rimsky is the client meeting someone else's requirement. `service_auth` is a two-mode switch, default off. Off, internal dials are plaintext on a trusted-subnet assumption. Under `mtls`, a per-deployment CA lives in the control plane, each standing service enrolls for a short-lived leaf certificate, and both services present and verify.

*Where you meet it:* Config key `service_auth`, and per-service `<service>.tls`. HTTP routes `POST /v1/enroll`, `GET /v1/ca-root`. Permission actions `service:enroll`, `service-auth:ca-root`. MCP tool `service_enroll`. Environment variables `RIMSKY_SERVICE_AUTH`, `RIMSKY_CA_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `RIMSKY_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_ENROLLMENT`. Port 8091 (the host-daemon proxy's service-facing mTLS listener).

Both enrollment routes are conditional on a deployment CA existing. On the zero-config default, and with `service_auth: none`, `POST /v1/enroll` and `GET /v1/ca-root` answer 404 — the router has no such path — even to a key granted exactly `service:enroll`.

**breakpoint** — A pause point installed at runtime on a live instance, bound to a matcher, a checkpoint position (pre-dispatch or post-terminal), an optional signal-type filter, a mode (pause or notify-only), an overflow policy, and an optional TTL. A pause-mode hit blocks the runner; you inspect the snapshot and resume, optionally with a one-shot overlay that merges onto the dispatch. An unresumed pause also opens the debug-override channel, which applies persistent attribute writes and invalidations against the paused instance. That channel is frame-scoped: it resolves "the node's latest run" within the instance's active frame only, and refuses a node whose runs belong to another frame.

*Where you meet it:* HTTP routes `POST /v1/instances/{idOrKey}/breakpoints`, `GET /v1/instances/{idOrKey}/breakpoints`, `DELETE /v1/instances/{idOrKey}/breakpoints/{breakpoint_id}`, `POST /v1/instances/{idOrKey}/breakpoints/{breakpoint_id}/resume`, `GET /v1/instances/{idOrKey}/breakpoint-hits`, `POST /v1/instances/{id}/debug/override`. MCP tools `breakpoint_create`, `breakpoint_list`, `breakpoint_delete`, `breakpoint_resume_hit`, `instance_debug_override`. MCP resources `rimsky://instances/{id}/breakpoint-hits`, `rimsky://breakpoints/{breakpoint_id}/hits`. Permission actions `breakpoint:read|create|resume|delete`, `instance:debug-override`. Event kinds `breakpoint.hit`, `debug.override.applied`. Bundled role `debug-operator`.

The debugger is HTTP and MCP only. `rimsky breakpoint` is not a command.

**event-log** (alias: audit log) — Rimsky's append-only record of what happened. Each row carries an id, the originating instance and node where the row is instance- or node-scoped, a typed `kind`, a JSON payload, and a timestamp. Kinds come from two families: 44 operational kinds, and the signal type-paths. Rimsky's supervisor, scheduler, and control API write rows at observable transitions. The `auth.*` subset has its own read surface, gated on `audit:read` and filterable by actor, action, target, result, mode, and time.

*Where you meet it:* CLI verbs `rimsky instance events`, `rimsky logs`, `rimsky watch`. HTTP routes `GET /v1/events`, `GET /v1/audit`, `GET /v1/observability/events`. MCP tools `event_list`, `audit_list`. Permission actions `event:read`, `audit:read`. 44 event kinds. Config key `retention.trace_trailing`.

Three properties shape how you query the feed. `kind` is an exact match, not a prefix: `claim`, `claim_`, and `auth.` are each rejected with 400, and `claim/` parses as a signal type-path, answers 200, and matches nothing — so a prefix guess can read as an empty feed rather than an error. Identifier coverage is not uniform: run-scoped kinds carry both instance and node, `instance_terminated` carries only an instance, and `auth.access_attempted` carries neither, so narrowing to one node drops those rows silently. And the kinds do not pair: `lock_acquired` has `lock_released`, but `subclaim.acquired` and `claim_acquired` have no release counterpart, and asking for one is rejected as an unknown kind.

**orphan-reaper** — A family of purpose-named sweeps, deliberately not unified, that reclaim orphaned work. The dispatch sweeps release orphaned claims back to the pending queue by clearing the claimant, rather than deleting rows; the claim-handle sweep hard-deletes expired handle rows. Synchronous dispatches key on the supervisor's outgoing connection state, so cleanup happens in band. Asynchronous and in-frame dispatches key on the run's progress timestamp against its quiet-period and total-runtime deadlines. The claim-handle sweep keys on a short renewed liveness lease instead. Every release and delete is guarded on the claimant, so a live owner is never clobbered.

*Where you meet it:* Config keys `dispatch_defaults.sync_rpc_deadline|max_quiet_period|max_runtime`. Template keys `nodes[].sync_rpc_deadline|max_quiet_period|max_runtime`. Event kinds `lock_orphan_reaped`, `orphaned_claim_released`, `orphaned_claim_lost_race`.

**supervisor** — One of the three runtime binaries: rimsky's worker side. It selects candidate work, performs the atomic acquisition transaction, calls the executor, handles the terminal, and fires the auto-terminal verbs. It registers itself at startup with its dispatch concurrency and the callback host and port executors dial back on. Its callback listener carries four per-run routes: the async terminal, a keepalive that bumps the progress timestamp, an attribute writeback that merges a delta and bumps the timestamp in one transaction, and a health probe. The keepalive and writeback routes authenticate on the dispatch's cancel token as a bearer credential.

*Where you meet it:* Binary `rimsky-supervisor`. Image command `rimsky-supervisor`. HTTP routes `POST /v1/callback/{async_ack_id}`, `POST /v1/runs/{run_id}/keepalive`, `POST /v1/runs/{run_id}/attributes`, `GET /health` on the callback listener. Config keys `rimsky.yml: supervisor.supervisor_id|supervisor.concurrency|supervisor.liveness_interval_ms|supervisor.claim_poll_interval_ms|supervisor.callback.host|supervisor.callback.port|supervisor.callback.advertise_host|supervisor.callback.advertise_port`. Environment variables `RIMSKY_SUPERVISOR_CALLBACK_ADVERTISE_HOST`, `RIMSKY_SUPERVISOR_CALLBACK_ADVERTISE_PORT`, `RIMSKY_CALLBACK_URL`, `RIMSKY_CALLBACK_TOKEN`, `RIMSKY_METRICS_PORT_SUPERVISOR`. Port 8081. Event kinds `work_started`, `work_completed`, `work_rejected`.

The callback listener binds on all interfaces, so executors need a reachable name to dial back: set `callback.advertise_host`. Its default port, 8081, sits in the core block, clear of every bundled service's default.

**replica** — One running process of a rimsky binary behind a load balancer. Rimsky does not model replicas: it does not detect them, heartbeat them, address them individually, or provide replica-aware coordination. The one exception is the scheduler's dispatch tick, which an advisory lock serializes to a single replica. Every other role behaves as N independent processes. Scaling is the operator's decision.

*Where you meet it:* Config key `supervisor.yml: supervisor_id`. Environment variable `RIMSKY_SCHEDULER_ID`. Binaries `rimsky-scheduler`, `rimsky-supervisor`, `rimsky-control-api`. Image commands of the same names.

**persistence-database** — The umbrella over rimsky's persistence layer: one database handle per process, opened once and held for the process's life. It hands back the queue, the per-ledger accessors, the advisory locker, the migration runner, a health check, and close. Two implementations sit behind it, chosen by `persistence.driver`: a client-server backend (Postgres) and an embedded file backend (SQLite). In the split deployment each of the three roles holds its own handle; in the all-in-one they share one.

*Where you meet it:* Config keys `persistence.driver`, `persistence.postgres.dsn|max_open_conns|min_conns|conn_max_lifetime`, `persistence.sqlite.path`. Binary `rimsky-migrate`. Environment variable `RIMSKY_ENTRYPOINT_MIGRATE`. Image path `/var/lib/rimsky/state.db`. HTTP routes `GET /v1/health`, `GET /v1/observability/system/health`.

The two backends are close but not interchangeable in every respect: a template driving the same work produces the same ids, the same event set, and the same read shapes on both, and a handful of retention and sweep behaviors differ. Migration is safe to re-run — a second boot over the same state applies nothing and comes up healthy — but there is no down or rollback path, and `rimsky-migrate` is not a role the image entrypoint accepts, so a one-shot job runs it through the CLI binary rather than `docker run … rimsky-migrate`.

**advisory-lock** — Five primitives on the persistence layer's advisory locker: a scheduler-tick lock, a migration lock, and three in-transaction locks keyed per name, per claim scope, and per lifecycle scope. The client-server backend uses native advisory locks. Under the embedded backend the first two are file locks beside the database file, and the three in-transaction locks are no-ops because the immediate-mode transaction's writer slot already subsumes them across processes. The tick lock makes the scheduler safe to run multi-replica; the migration lock serializes migrate runs; the in-transaction locks close race windows in acquisition and lifecycle fan-out.

*Where you meet it:* Config key `persistence.driver` selects which implementation runs. No element names an individual lock: the primitives are internal machinery, visible only in their effects — one scheduler tick at a time, one migrate run at a time.

**inertness** (alias: inert bytes) — The discipline that keeps rimsky project-agnostic: rimsky carries payloads without interpreting them. It governs seven carrier streams — claim scope, claim address, claim payload, attribute values, message bodies, executor scratch, and executor error payloads — in two strengths. **Byte-opaque** streams (scope, address, payload, scratch) rimsky reads only at a substitution leaf, at the byte-equality conflict comparison, or to put them on the executor's wire. **Structurally inert** streams (attribute values, message bodies, error payloads) rimsky may traverse for transport and for two content-matching sites — the matcher's equality check against one named path, and a subscription's CEL predicate over the signal payload. Rimsky never logs, formats, normalizes, indexes, or puts these bytes in an error message. The same leveling extends to vocabulary: executor-private state rides the generic carriers, chiefly scratch, and rimsky's own tables carry no executor-specific fields.

*Where you meet it:* Template keys `nodes[].claim_producers[].data`, `messages[].body_schema`, `nodes[].attributes.schema`. Substitution sources `{{claim.<alias>.payload...}}`, `{{messages.<type>...}}`. Executor scratch, carried on the settling outcome.

**module-layout** (alias: workspace-layout) — How rimsky's code is grouped, which matters to you only as an implementer. Four Go modules sit in one workspace. The **protocols** module is the single public module a service implementer imports: the protocol interfaces, the protobuf bindings, the server-side and publisher-side scaffolding, and the conformance library, on a deliberately small dependency budget. The **foundation** module holds primitives. The **services** module holds the bundled service implementations, which depend only on protocols. The **root** module holds the graph, runtime, and control layers plus the binaries, and pulls the heavier libraries an implementer never sees.

*Where you meet it:* Published packages `github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core/lib/protocols` (the module to import), `github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core`, and `@rimsky-ai/protocols` on npm. Proto files: all ten.

The npm package is proto files, not generated code. It contains ten `.proto` files and exports exactly `protoDir` and `protoPath`, so a TypeScript implementer runs protoc themselves.

---

## Two notes on what ships

**Images are single-architecture.** All fifteen published images carry one platform, `linux/arm64`, and none is a multi-platform index. The release archives do ship four `{linux,darwin}_{amd64,arm64}` combinations, so the CLI binary and the images differ here.

**Only two protocols have an HTTP+JSON bridge.** The claim-producer and executor protocols speak HTTP+JSON: `rimsky conformance claim-producer --transport http` runs the full battery against a bundled producer's bridge, and rimsky itself dispatches to an executor declared `transport: http`. The other protocols are gRPC only, whatever the `transport` selector and the bridge ports suggest.
